extracted.intended_audience: government and military legal officers, procurement officials, and patent counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and administrative rules governing patents as they relate to United States government use, procurement, officer-employee inventions, royalties, assignments, infringement risk, and compensation. Covers presumptions of validity, liens, indemnities in contracts, and special rules for government employees and military officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant of letters patent is prima facie evidence of inventorship and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption in favor of the validity of a patent, arising from the action of the authorities in granting it, can be overcome only by reliable and certain proof. The grant of letters patent is prima facie evidence that the patentee was the first inventor of the device described in the letters, and of its novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (e.g., Cantrell v. Wallick). Example application: a third party's affidavits alleging prior invention do not impugn a patent where the party took no action to contest issuance or seek remedy in courts (P. 63, 416, May, 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use with patentee's knowledge implies obligation to pay reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of a patent with the knowledge and consent of the patentee is an implied promise or agreement to pay for the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites decisions and departmental cases (C. 725, Dec. 1894; 6107, Mar. 23, 1899; 8321, Aug. 20, 1900; 22877, Mar. 10, 1908). Practical effect: government use with patentee consent can create an obligation to compensate by royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing royalty is a legal lien on the patented article
rubrics_metrics.description: An existing royalty on a patented article is in the nature of a legal lien upon it, to be paid off before it can be safely used, and is also an element properly entering into the price to be paid for it, if purchased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, when the United States purchases a patented article for public works it should pay a price estimated by intrinsic value augmented by probable royalties (P. 141, 358, Dec. 1890; C. 8321, Aug. 20, 1900; 17647, Mar. 10, 1905). The article is sold subject to the royalty claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of patented right to United States does not necessarily preclude foreign assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: The assignment to the United States of a patent right, for use in the public service, does not preclude the assignor from also assigning the right to a foreign government, provided the original assignment were not absolute in its terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendation: as a general rule the United States should accept nothing short of an absolute assignment when required (P. 54, 214, June, 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting when contractor's proposed work may infringe requires indemnity and bond
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bidder proposes to use a machine that is subject to suit for patent infringement, the United States should require a clause that: if legal proceedings arise against the United States during execution, the contractor shall hold the United States harmless and refund all expenses, damages and outlays; and if proceedings cause delay, the United States may employ others to complete the work and claim extra costs from the contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites decisions (C. 725, Dec. 1894; 4558, July 1898; 23546, July 3, 1908). Also practical drafting language and indemnity/bonding for government contracts are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor serving on a board considering his invention is disallowed but purchase still permitted
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a violation of law (act of Feb. 18, 1893) for the inventor of a device considered and adopted by a Board to be a member or serve on that Board; however, where he has in fact served, the act does not prohibit the purchase of the instrument invented by him—it affects eligibility for membership/service only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited (G. 6941, Aug., 1899). Distinguishes conflict-of-interest in membership from the separate procurement question.

rubrics_metrics.name: An unpatented (or patent-applied-for) invention is property and may be enjoined
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is property though it be not patented, and an injunction will be granted to restrain an infringement although the patent has been merely applied for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: the United States should be cautious buying from someone other than the inventor because it may be liable to the real patentee for damages even if it did not know of infringement at time of purchase (P. 43, 264, Oct., 1890; P. 57, 297, Jan., 1893). The government becomes a tort-feasor in permitting use of an infringed patent (C. 725, Dec., 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer-patents and government use when patented without fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of March 3, 1883, an officer of the Army is entitled to issuance of a patent without any fee for certain classes of inventions, and if so patented the United States is entitled to use the patent without payment of royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statute and decision (G. 12517, Apr. 28, 1902). Practical effect: special rule for military officers' inventions; government use without royalty when lawfully patented under statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-employee inventions made in line of duty grant government implied license
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a person in the employ of the United States, using Government time and funds for the purpose and in the line of his duty, makes an invention and patents it, the Government has an implied license to use the invention with an unrestricted right to manufacture it or have it manufactured for its use; but where a government employee not specifically employed for the purpose makes an invention he is entitled to the benefits of the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and cases cited (P. 31, 106, Mar. 15, 1889; G. 25188, June 25–Oct. 31, 1910; decisions relating to particular devices and processes). Distinguishes inventions made in scope of employment from outside inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of June 25, 1910: compensation right and limits for patentees whose patents are used by US
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of June 25, 1910 gives to a bona fide patentee a right to recover reasonable compensation for an article patented by him which is used by the United States, but enables the United States to avail itself of any and all defenses which might be pleaded by a defendant in an action for infringement; it also provides that benefits shall not inure to a patentee who, at the time of making his claim, is in the employment or service of the United States and made the device during his employment; the act applies to assignees as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites statute and decision (C. 27038, July 15, 1910). Practical implication: claim process exists but limited by statutory defenses and employee-exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using an infringed patent in Government service creates tort liability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government becomes a tort-feasor in permitting the use in its service of an infringed patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites case law (C. 725, Dec., 1894) and supports the recommendation to secure proper assignments/clear title or indemnities when procuring patented articles; cross-reference to Schillinger and other Supreme Court cases noted in text.
